source.title: Mitigating LLM Over-Refusal via Dynamic Semantic Routing Calibration
source.authors: Zi-Xuan Wang; Bing-Jie Zhang; He Zhao; Dan-Dan Guo

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether intervening on a selected subset of attention heads changes refusal-related behavior, using head suppression and behavioral rates rather than the original fine-tuning or token-KL methods.
record.gate_note: The study tests V5 through head-suppression ablations with over-refusal and safety-rate outcomes in Table 11. It does not test harmful or benign fine-tuning as claimed in V1–V2, aligned/base per-token KL in V3, compliant-prefill or suffix bypass in V4, or training that deepens safety in V6–V7. Table 1 and other full-method comparisons combine head intervention with additional SRC components; they are not extracted as evidence isolating the localized heads. The reported OR-Bench-augmented training result measures benign-prompt compliance, not harmful compliance.
record.test_reason: The paper's aim is over-refusal mitigation, but Table 11 (Appendix D.6) reports harmful-request safety rates after scaling the value outputs of specific attention-head subsets by negative α. For generic safety heads from Zhou et al. 2025, safety falls from 99% to 40–45%. That is a weak, head-level result bearing on V5. It comes from a single unstated model (likely LLaMA-3-8B, per Figure 10), the generic-head count is unstated, and there is no uncertainty. The over-refusal rows measure refusal of benign prompts, not safety behaviour, so they do not bear on V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also claim Table 11 shows over-refusal stems from a specific subset of semantic-routing heads, distinct from generic safety heads whose suppression collapses safety. They state that SRC relieves over-refusal while largely preserving safety.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses inference-time attention-head suppression and dual-branch logits fusion, rather than fine-tuning on examples or measuring aligned/base per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Head identity and intervention strength affect the safety–over-refusal trade-off. The paper also reports sensitivity to head-localization choices and dataset size, and evaluates SRC under greedy and nucleus sampling; those results do not test V4's proposed decoding bypass.

fits_no_version.finding: Negatively scaling noun-attention-selected heads reduces over-refusal on benign prompts (52%→10–13%), more efficiently than generic or lower-ranked heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over-refusal on benign but safety-sounding prompts is carried by a sparse set of mid-layer attention heads.

fits_no_version.finding: Hard-Safe prompts show lower noun-token attention and higher attention entropy than Safe or Unsafe prompts in Qwen2.5-7B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over-refusal is associated with disrupted noun-centric attention routing.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Table 11 does not state the evaluated model or dataset in the supplied text. The study reports no uncertainty estimates for these rates. The authors note that head localization depends on the diversity and coverage of its samples, that multi-turn and long-context settings are underexplored, and that excessive intervention can degrade harmful-request refusal.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's SRC benchmark scores and Tables 2–4, 6, 9–10 compare or ablate the full framework, system prompts, training baselines, or decoding configurations rather than isolating the V5 head-localization claim. Table 4's OR-Bench augmentation reports benign-prompt compliance but no harmful-compliance result. Figure-only plots beyond the explicitly described noun-attention and entropy findings were not extracted.

untested.parts: Benign fine-tuning effects on harmful compliance are not studied. The OR-Bench-augmented STL result measures over-refusal only.
No aligned-vs-base per-token KL is reported.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding bypass of the unmodified model. Table 13's role-play prefix evaluates SRC, not the baseline model.
Weight- or rank-level localization; how many generic heads carry safety; models other than the one in Table 11; true zero-ablation rather than negative scaling.
Causes of shallowness are not tested. The SFT-shortcut account in Section 3 is asserted, not tested.

missing.what: Table 11's evaluated model and safety benchmark are not stated; Figure 10 ties the ablation to LLaMA-3-8B. Rows should record this as inferred.

record.verdict_notes: Weak V5 evidence. The intervention multiplies head value outputs by negative α (a sign flip), not zero-ablation, so it is stronger than removal. Generic-head count, model and benchmark are unstated for Table 11, and no uncertainty is reported. The study's purpose is mitigation, so most rows are its own method's performance. The safety-rate rows are the only ones bearing on V5.

versions.untested_parts: Whether harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples raises harmful-request compliance.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning raises harmful-request compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Whether compliant prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes bypass refusal. The paper compares SRC and a baseline under decoding settings but does not test these as bypasses.
The study suppresses selected attention-head outputs; it does not establish that a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior generally, or test weight/rank edits.
Whether training data or the training objective causes safety behavior to be shallow.
Training that spreads safety beyond early response tokens and whether that training remains robust.

relationships.reason: Negatively scaling a head subset collapses harmful-request safety from 99% to 45% and 40% (R18, R20); the drop is 99→68 at α=-0.5 (R16).

relationships.condition: Heads selected by Hard-Safe/Unsafe noun-attention score (Top-64, ranks 64–128)
relationships.reason: Safety loss depends on which heads are chosen and how strongly they are scaled. It is modest (99→88/85/75, R4/R6/R8) and near zero for ranks 64–128 at α=-0.5 (96, R10). Large loss appears only at α=-2.0 (57, R14).
relationships.display_finding: Safety loss was modest (99 to 88, 85 or 75) and near zero for heads ranked 64–128 at α=-0.5 (96); a large loss appeared only at α=-2.0 (57).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Primary hypersensitive heads (Top-64), reported intervention strengths
reader_labels.reason: Suppressing the selected subset changes both over-refusal and safety rates; the reported over-refusal rates fall from 52% to 13%, 11%, and 10% (R3, R5, R7), with corresponding safety rates of 88%, 85%, and 75% (R4, R6, R8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Lower-ranked or generic safety-related head sets, and stronger intervention settings
reader_labels.reason: Results depend on which heads are suppressed and the strength: lower-ranked heads produce a less complete over-refusal reduction, while generic-head suppression and stronger edits carry substantial safety-rate costs (R9–R20).
